newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Maine Yankee has long way to go for start up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Maine Yankee has long way to go for start up.

text.p: U.S. nuclear regulators and Maine Yankee officials said Tuesday they could not predict when the company's troubled nuclear plant in Wiscasset, Maine, would be able to restart operations.

"We can't give a date," Nuclear Regulatory Commissin Chairwoman Shirley Jackson said after a briefing by Maine Yankee to the NRC about the company's hiring of new managers and efforts to fix serious equipment problems.
The 910-megawatt plant, supplier of about a quarter of Maine's electricity, has been shut since December because of an electrical cable problem affecting back-up systems.
"I wouldn't want to be in the mode of predicting a (start-up) schedule at the moment," Maine Yankee vice president of operations Graham Leitch said. "Our focus has to be on safety."
The commission put the plant on its watchlist of unsafe plants last week, a year after stepping up inspections there. The plant has been shut repeatedly over the last two years.

The NRC has already notified Maine Yankee that before restarting operations, it will have to show the commission that it has corrected problems with electrical cables, off-site power systems, and design configurations.
Leitch said he expected the NRC to raise even more issues as prerequisites to restarting as more problems came to light.
"It's impossible to know yet all of what is needed," said NRC regional administrator Hubert Miller.
Jackson said the commission was partly to blame for failing to prevent or clamp down on problems earlier. "Yes, we accept some responsibility for what happened," she told reporters.
The commission has come under heavy criticism over the last year for weak regulation of the industry.
Among 3,200 issues raised in a broad NRC inspection of Maine Yankee last year were design weaknesses that Jackson said were "not part of the regular inspection program."
However, the NRC also blamed Maine Yankee for letting equipment maintenance slide in order to cut costs.
"They have had a focus on economics that impacted how vigorously and rigorously they've gone after some of those design basis issues," Jackson said.
In response to the plant's problems, Maine Yankee last month took the unusual step of appointing an outside company, Entergy Corp, to manage operations at the plant.
Entergy officials told the commission they would start developing an improvement plan for the facility next week.
Mike Sellman, recently named president-elect of Maine Yankee, said Entergy would take steps to reduce maintenance backlogs and replace equipment that was obsolete.

Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, seven percent by Bangor Hydro-Electric Co, five percent by Maine Public Service Co, and 10 percent by other New England utilities.
